doc.title: Albert Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

title: Jazz as orchestrated blues; blues are about love, not politics
summary: Murray calls jazz a fully orchestrated blues statement and argues the blues concern love and a good time, not discrimination or politics, citing church preachers.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: You often read the idea that people call jazz the only true American art form, and I’m wondering, are they separating blues from that do you feel? Blues is certainly an American art form. We were talking earlier about how it’s a synthesis of what people experience in this country.

See I just see jazz as a fully orchestrated blues statement. I mean if you say blues, generally people are talking about folk blues. And that’s a very limited art form. But as extended, elaborated and refined by the most inventive musicians in the idiom which created the blues, you have jazz. The function of jazz of course is always to get rid of the blues, that is the blues as such, you know, having the blues. But blues music, most people are talking about a folk form and most people who deal with it don’t know anything about it, they just have made up their minds and basically their conception comes from sociology and political history and things like that that have nothing to do with the existential problems that the blues is concerned with. I don’t understand that, really, © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

because there’s very little in the blues that has to do with political situations. You know it’s really a ridiculous type thing, a position where college professors and writers and so forth impose study on something which has nothing to do with what the blues musician is doing. The musician lives on the level of existential preoccupation. He is concerned with the quality of life. He’s not concerned with forms of government, economics, discrimination, things like that are not part of our subjects of the blues. And people keep acting as if they were. They are not. They’re about — the lyric poetry of almost any culture has to do with love. But blues is about love, about the relationship of men and women, about betrayal. If you get money, it’s only about a love story, it’s about somebody who’s going with this girl and then he lost his job or he couldn’t give her an expensive presents and he had to be the type of person who loved her. It’s not talking about discrimination and racism and things like that. I know very few blues musicians that are concerned with that. They’re concerned with a good time, having a good time, they play the blues in honky tonks and places like that, not when people are out in a bad mood, but when they’re looking for fun. And yet we get all this talk about it as if that’s what it’s about. All you have to do is to go to any church and listen to the preacher talk about the blues. And he calls it “good time music.” He does not say this is the music that’s commensurate with this. The church didn’t even deal with that 40 years ago. I mean I’ve never been to a church where the preacher prayed to God to change the white people. I’ve never heard a sermon in which they asked the Lord to stop prejudice. I’ve never heard a preacher preach that way to God, talking to God. There’s all these people and they’re talking to God in church. I’ve never heard them say that. I was a big boy, in high school and so forth, during the depression, in high school and in college, and I never heard anybody pray to let the stock market go up or something. You see? I don’t know where all this stuff comes from. I’m concerned with what art does as an existential function of the intrinsic quality of life at a given time you see? And you get somebody else come in and they just listen and they talk, but they’re not doing anything that’s different. They’re going to a honky tonk. If you want to hear the blues, they don’t go to church to talk about injustice. When they go to church they talk about their soul after death, and whether or not they’re going to qualify to enter the pearly gates. And I don’t know any musician, unless he was seduced by people during the Communism binge that you know they came out of the depression, and then they write some lyrics for them to sing, but that’s not aphrodisiac. The blues is aphrodisiac. You can’t have a parallel of the blues and the socio-political position of the Negroes in the United States. It just isn’t there. People want to put it there but it isn’t. That’s not what blues is about. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
